NFL Black Friday and Christmas Games: How Sportsbooks Price the League's Newest Holiday Windows

Published November 6, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Thanksgiving has been a fixture on the NFL calendar since long before sports betting was legal in a single US state, and our guide to Thanksgiving pricing covers why those three games get treated differently than a normal Thursday slate. Black Friday and Christmas Day are a newer story. Amazon's standalone Black Friday game debuted in 2023, and Netflix's multi-year Christmas Day package followed in 2024, and both have already settled into pricing patterns that look nothing like a typical regular-season Sunday. Neither window exists because of football logic — both exist because streaming platforms pay well for a captive, no-competition audience — and that commercial origin story is exactly why the betting markets around them behave a little strangely.

Why these windows exist at all

For decades, the only guaranteed NFL games outside the normal Sunday/Monday/Thursday rotation were the three Thanksgiving games and an occasional Christmas game slotted into whatever day of the week the holiday happened to land on. That changed once streaming services started treating the NFL as a subscriber-acquisition tool rather than just a content library. Amazon had already proven with Thursday Night Football that a standalone streaming window could pull in double-digit-million viewership, and when the league floated a Black Friday slot — a day with essentially no competing live sports and a national audience already off work — Amazon took it. Netflix followed a similar logic for Christmas Day, signing a multi-year deal that put the league's games in front of a subscriber base of hundreds of millions of accounts in a day otherwise owned by holiday movies and specials.

The pattern to notice: both windows were created for reach, not for competitive balance. The league fills them with games expected to have broad appeal, which is a different selection process than how a normal week's schedule gets built — and that difference shows up in how early and how confidently the market can price them.

Black Friday: one game, zero competition

The standalone Black Friday game sits in an early afternoon window on a day when it's the only professional football being played anywhere. That's a meaningfully different setup than even a marquee Sunday night game, which still has to share the week with a full slate of early and late Sunday windows. A Black Friday game effectively absorbs a full day's worth of NFL betting interest into one game, which has two practical effects on the market: total-market liquidity on that single game runs unusually high for a single-game slate, and the mix of money leans more recreational than a typical game, since a chunk of the audience is casual viewers who tuned in for the event rather than regulars following that specific matchup all season.

There's also a timing wrinkle worth knowing about. Because the networks want to announce their showcase games well ahead of the season for marketing purposes, the Black Friday matchup is often locked in months before kickoff, before anyone knows which of the two teams will actually be good that November. That's the same dynamic our look-ahead lines guide describes on a weekly scale, except here it plays out over an entire offseason — a team picked for its market size or roster hype in the spring can turn out to be a bottom-feeder by the holiday, and the opening numbers on that game sometimes need bigger in-season corrections than a line set the way every other week's matchup normally is.

Christmas: more games, a compressed stretch

Christmas Day pricing has its own quirks, mostly because the day itself doesn't fall on a fixed day of the week. When the holiday lands on a weekday, the league has leaned on Saturday windows the week before to keep the rest of its Week 16 inventory from getting squeezed out, which means some years include an unusually dense run of games across Thanksgiving, a mid-December Saturday slate, and Christmas itself, all inside about a month. The number of games actually played on December 25 has varied by year under the current deal — sometimes a single marquee game, sometimes a doubleheader split between two platforms — and the league has made clear it's more interested in flexibility to chase ratings than in locking the format in permanently.

From a betting standpoint, a Christmas game carries a lot of the same "showcase audience" pricing behavior as Black Friday: elevated total handle for a single game, a bettor pool skewed more toward casual action, and plenty of attention on player props given how many new fans are tuning in specifically to catch star names. What makes Christmas different is the scheduling ripple effect it creates across the rest of that week's slate, which is where the real pricing story is.

The hidden cost: a bunched-up rest calendar

Our guide to short-week Thursday games covers how a compressed turnaround moves a single line. The Thanksgiving-to-Christmas stretch is a version of that problem repeated across several weeks for a handful of teams rather than a one-off event. A team that plays on Thanksgiving Thursday is already working on short rest heading into the following Sunday. If the league also shifts some of that team's Week 16 games to Saturday to make room for Christmas inventory, and the team then draws a Christmas Day assignment itself, it can end up stacking two or three short-turnaround games inside a single month — a workload pattern that simply didn't exist before these extra holiday windows were created.

StretchTypical rest between gamesBetting-relevant effect
Normal Sunday-to-Sunday week7 daysBaseline; no rest-driven adjustment needed
Thanksgiving Thursday game4 days (if playing the prior Sunday)Short-week fatigue priced into that one game
Week 16 Saturday game (holiday-driven)5-6 days, varies by prior slotMild rest compression, usually smaller line impact
Christmas Day assignment following a Saturday Week 16 gameAs few as 6 days twice in a rowCumulative fatigue risk across two straight shortened weeks

No single part of that stretch is dramatic on its own, which is exactly why it's easy to miss. A market that's pricing in one short week correctly can still underweight the compounding effect of a team working through its second or third abbreviated turnaround of the season in the span of four weeks, especially late in the year when injuries have already thinned a roster.

Worth tracking: before betting a Christmas or late-December game, it's worth checking not just that week's rest split but how many short-week games each team has already absorbed since Thanksgiving. A team on its third compressed week in a month is a different team than one coming off a normal bye-to-bye schedule, even if the public line doesn't always reflect that gap.

What this means when you're reading the line

None of this means Black Friday or Christmas lines are mispriced in any exploitable, consistent way — sportsbooks are well aware of all of the factors above and build them into the number. What it does mean is that these two games deserve a different read than a standard Sunday matchup. A Black Friday line should be weighed with its months-old scheduling origin in mind rather than assumed to reflect the same in-season information every other Week 12 or 13 line has. A Christmas game is worth checking against each team's recent rest history rather than just that week's in isolation. Treat both less like "just another game with extra hype" and more like what they actually are: matchups the league picked for business reasons first, with a scheduling ripple effect that normal weeks don't carry.

Frequently asked questions

Has the NFL always played on Christmas Day?

Occasionally, yes — the league has slotted games onto December 25 going back decades whenever it happened to fall on a game day. What's new is the dedicated, multi-year streaming package that treats Christmas as its own standalone broadcast event rather than an incidental date on the calendar.

Is the Black Friday game chosen based on which teams are playing well?

No. Like most showcase broadcast windows, the matchup is typically locked in well before the season for marketing and ratings reasons, not current form. That's part of why the opening line on that game can need more in-season correction than a line set the normal way, closer to kickoff.

Do Black Friday and Christmas games see more public betting than a normal game?

Generally yes. Both windows pull in a broader, more casual national audience than a typical regular-season game, and that tends to skew the betting pool more toward recreational, public-side action than a book would see on an average Sunday matchup.

Does playing on Christmas hurt a team's rest more than a normal week?

It depends on the calendar that year. When the holiday falls on a weekday and the league shifts other Week 16 games to Saturday to make room, teams involved in that reshuffling can end up with back-to-back short-rest weeks, which is a bigger factor than the Christmas game itself in isolation.

Should I treat a Black Friday or Christmas total the same way I'd treat a Thanksgiving total?

They share some of the same "showcase audience" betting patterns, but Thanksgiving is a three-game, decades-studied window, while Black Friday and Christmas are newer, lower-sample events with their own scheduling quirks. Treat the comparison as a useful starting point, not an exact match.
